claims.text: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has 20 at.% each of Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, and Ti.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy is a homogenized, single-phase FCC solid solution.
The as-cast CoCrFeNiTi state is comparatively disordered and has little short-range order.
Near-random atomic arrangements provide lower barriers to dislocation motion than locally ordered arrangements.
Low barriers to dislocation motion cause the starting alloy to have low strength and hardness.
Low barriers to dislocation motion cause high ductility and machinability in the starting alloy.
Annealing equimolar CoCrFeNiTi at 600 °C for 10–100 hours will progressively increase its short-range order.
The proposed 600 °C anneals can induce short-range order without forming long-range order or secondary phases.
Short-range or local chemical order creates spatial heterogeneities that increase activation barriers for dislocation motion.
Short-range order increases localized lattice distortion in CoCrFeNiTi.
Ordering-induced obstacles increase critical shear stress and therefore raise yield strength.
Increasing short-range order will raise the hardness of CoCrFeNiTi.
Increasing short-range order will moderately reduce the plastic strain or ductility of CoCrFeNiTi.
Hardness and yield strength will increase monotonically with annealing duration because short-range order increases with duration.
The proposed mechanism applies only while CoCrFeNiTi remains a single-phase FCC solid solution.
The hypothesis is limited to testing from room temperature to 600 °C and to no more than 10% plastic strain.
A controlled comparison of identically prepared unannealed and annealed samples can test whether measured short-range order correlates with hardness, yield strength, and ductility.
Failure to increase hardness or yield strength after a confirmed increase in short-range order, in the absence of secondary phases, would falsify the proposed strengthening mechanism.

contradictions.description: The starting material is called both 'as-cast' and 'homogenized.' Homogenization is a post-casting heat treatment, so the thermal history and corresponding initial ordering state are not defined consistently.

The boundary restricts the hypothesis to samples without long-range order or secondary phases, whereas the falsification rule treats formation of such phases as falsification. Phase formation instead places the experiment outside the stated domain and confounds attribution to SRO.
